headline: High: shared filesystem and permissive tool use create prompt-injection, leakage, and write-conflict risks; Windsurf’s auto-execute can amplify ms-swift outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ms-swift reads/writes files and emits outputs over stdin/stdout, while Windsurf uses clipboard, workspace files, and MCP servers. That creates a plausible bridge where content from one can be treated as instructions by the other. The interaction is not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF ms-swift output is copied into Windsurf chat or workspace files
IF Windsurf ingests workspace content or MCP output as instructions
mitigations: Disable copy-paste of agent outputs into prompts
Separate workspaces for the two agents
Require provenance tags on imported text
Turn off MCP servers for the shared session
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization/provenance filtering

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and Windsurf shares state via the local filesystem. ms-swift handles hub_token and sdk-token, so a shared workspace could expose sensitive files or logs to Windsurf. Because the pairwise data-flow is inferred from profiles rather than directly observed, medium is the appropriate conservative choice.
conditions: IF ms-swift stores tokens, logs, or checkpoints in a shared directory
IF Windsurf opens or indexes that shared directory
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared workspaces
Restrict Windsurf to a separate project folder
Rotate any exposed tokens
Review and redact logs before sharing
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ms-swift can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, and Windsurf can also write the filesystem, modify git state, and auto-execute terminal commands. With shared local filesystem state, concurrent edits can overwrite each other or corrupt git/workspace state. The overlap is directly supported by both profiles, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory
IF Windsurf auto-execute is enabled or ms-swift writes concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Disable auto-execute in Windsurf
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git branches per agent
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transaction coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: ms-swift can generate files, logs, and training outputs that Windsurf may treat as authoritative workspace input. Windsurf’s agentic IDE loop and terminal execution can then act on those outputs without an explicit verification step. That creates a realistic path from one agent’s mistaken output to downstream irreversible actions.
conditions: IF Windsurf uses ms-swift-produced files as source-of-truth
IF Cascade auto-execute is enabled or commands are approved without review
mitigations: Require human review before acting on generated files
Mark ms-swift outputs as untrusted
Disable auto-execute
Use a validation step before commits or commands
requires-engineering: add schema checks for agent-generated artifacts

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift handles hub_token and sdk-token and touches datasets, checkpoints, and evaluation outputs, while Windsurf handles model provider keys and workspace files. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because the data classes differ and the evidence is incomplete, medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace
IF either agent logs or retains that data beyond policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Review retention settings for both tools
Avoid storing secrets in agent-visible files
Document data-handling boundaries
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
